book.title: The AI Ready School
book.author: Stephen R. Jordan

name: Translation With Human Review
title: Translation With Human Review
answer: Translation with human review means using machine translation for everyday school messages while having a fluent person check anything critical before it goes to families. It matters because translation tools widen communication with families who were once left out, but their errors can change meaning in high-stakes situations. The book's rule is routine messages through a tool, critical messages through a person.

sections.body: Machine translation can help schools reach families in many languages, and tools such as TalkingPoints and Microsoft Translator can translate messages, documents, and speech in both directions. This has brought in families who previously had little communication with the school. The problem is that these tools are not perfect, and mistakes can matter when the message concerns safety, discipline, or a student's special education. The idea solves that by treating machine translation as a first draft for routine contact and reserving human review for messages where an error could cause real harm. It also asks districts to plan who will review messages in each major home language rather than leaving review to chance.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a school can send a reminder about picture day through a translation tool because the message is routine and low risk. A notice about a safety incident, a disciplinary hearing, or a special education meeting should be reviewed by a fluent person before it is sent. The text does not give separate steps by grade band, so the same rule applies across elementary, middle, and high school communication. Districts should name reviewers for each major home language in the community so that critical messages have a known person to check them. Schools should also check their state requirements for translation and interpretation, because local duties can go beyond the federal rules.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book points to research in health care to show the risks. A review of 27 studies found that machine translation works best on simple sentences and in widely spoken European languages, and it recommended treating machine translation as a first draft to be corrected by a person (Dew et al., 2018). A review of 18 studies found serious errors in a majority of them, with accuracy lower for languages such as Haitian Creole and Vietnamese (Strechen et al., 2025). The book states that schools face the same limits, so the health care findings are used as a warning about school communication rather than as a school-specific study.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are clear: machine translation is not perfect, and errors can matter. Routine messages may go through a tool, but critical messages should be reviewed by a fluent person before they are sent. The decision about which messages are critical stays with people, as does the choice of who is fluent enough to review each language. Districts should name reviewers for each major home language, and they should check state requirements for translation and interpretation. Schools' legal duties to families with limited English continue even as federal guidance has changed, and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act still applies to how schools serve English learners and their families (Hardin, 2025).
